rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The marriage prohibitions and permissions in 4:22–25 reinstate marital laws established by earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: The prohibitions and permissions regarding marriage detailed in vv.22–25 are considered to be a reinstatement of marital laws established by previous prophets (Ṭ, Z).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who follow lusts may mean fornicators specifically, or more broadly people who follow desire instead of religious prescriptions.
rows.anchor: Those who follow lusts (v. 27) may refer explicitly to fornicators or more generally to those who follow their desires instead of the prescriptions of religion.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Minority traditions identify those following lusts with Jews or other People of the Book, or Zoroastrians, said to allow more marriage partners, including nieces.
rows.anchor: Minority traditions suggest that these may be references to the People of the Book, particularly Jews, or Zoroastrians, who reportedly had a less restrictive view of legitimate marriage partners (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: God lightens the burden by allowing men without sufficient means to marry enslaved women.
rows.anchor: allowing men of insufficient means to marry slave women—for man was created weak

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Human weakness here is a generally limited capacity to resist sexual desire and attraction to women for long.
rows.anchor: with a generally weak capacity to resist sexual desire and attraction to women for long (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also describes God lightening the burden for Muslims in other ways.
rows.anchor: The Quran mentions that God lightened the burden for Muslims in other ways (8:66)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accommodations for human weakness include marital relations on Ramadan nights and a reduction of daily prayers at the Prophet’s request during the Night Journey.
rows.anchor: similar accommodations for human weakness are implied in permitting sexual relations between spouses on the nights of Ramadan (2:187) and in God’s reducing the number of daily prayers at the Prophet’s request during the Night Journey (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s desire for ease for servants is stated elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: The Quran states that God desires ease for His servants (2:185)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslim religious obligations are easier than those of earlier communities and obligations they imposed on themselves.
rows.anchor: other verses indicate that the religious obligations of Muslims are easier than those of earlier communities (7:157) and those they impose on themselves (3:93).

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās counts verses 26–28 among eight verses in the sūrah demonstrating God’s mercy toward humanity, alongside verses 31, 40, 48, 110, and 147.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās considered vv. 26–28 to be among the eight important verses in this sūrah that demonstrate God’s Mercy toward human beings (the others are vv. 31, 40, 48, 110, 147; R, Z).

words: لِتَحْكُمَ بَيْنَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِمَآ أَرَىٰكَ ٱللَّهُ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One purpose of revelation was to enable the Prophet to judge among people according to what God had taught him.
rows.anchor: one of the purposes of the revelation to the Prophet was that he might judge between men according to what God has shown him—that is, according to what God has taught him (R).

words: لِتَحْكُمَ بَيْنَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِمَآ أَرَىٰكَ ٱللَّهُ
rows.speaker: Some scholars
rows.claim: Some scholars cite this wording as evidence that the Prophet could perform ijtihād by deriving rulings from Quranic principles and laws.
rows.anchor: Some scholars adduce this phrase to demonstrate that the Prophet had been given permission to perform ijtihād—that is, to derive independent rulings from the principles and laws contained in the Quran (IK).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses reportedly concern Ṭuʿmah ibn Ubayriq, likely a hypocrite, who stole armor, hid it among a Madinan Jew’s belongings, and accused him; after relatives solicited the Prophet’s defense, revelation warned him and directed him to seek forgiveness.
rows.anchor: at the behest of the latter’s relatives, but in v. 105 he was warned not to defend

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parallel between betraying trusts and betraying oneself concerns the same people and reflects that moral actions ultimately affect the actor.
rows.anchor: The parallelism between those who betray their trust in v. 105 and those who betray their own selves in v. 107, which both refer to the same people, reflects the Quranic idea that one’s moral or immoral actions ultimately affect only oneself (see v. 111).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly says that God does not wrong people; people wrong themselves.
rows.anchor: Hence the assertion found throughout the Quran in relation to wrongdoers that God does not wrong people, but that they wrong themselves (see, e.g., 2:57; 3:117; 7:160).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must apply Quranic rulings without favoritism, even when a nominal fellow Muslim is opposed to a member of another religious community.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is instructed to apply the rulings of the Quran without favoritism toward anyone—even on behalf of a (perhaps nominal) fellow Muslim against a member of another religious community (R).

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some argue that the warnings and forgiveness command imply the Prophet initially intended to advocate for Ṭuʿmah, which would challenge the doctrine that prophets are protected from major sins.
rows.anchor: a few have argued that these verses indicate that the Prophet was initially willing to advocate for the lying

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī replies that the Prophet was concerned and willing to get involved but took no decisive action while awaiting revelation, so the report does not establish a sinful defense.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī responds to this argument by noting that the report of this incident indicates that, although the Prophet was concerned about the situation and willing to get involved, he took no decisive action right away

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reports al-Rāzī’s further reading that the command to seek forgiveness could mean seeking forgiveness for those who tried to persuade the Prophet to advocate for Ṭuʿmah.
rows.anchor: The instruction to the Prophet to seek forgiveness of God, he further argues, may be read as an instruction to seek forgiveness for others—namely, for those who tried to persuade him to advocate for Ṭuʿmah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s bounty and mercy here mean that He revealed Ṭuʿmah’s guilt, stopping the clansmen’s attempt to mislead the Prophet into pardoning and interceding for their guilty kinsman.
rows.anchor: understood to mean in this context that He revealed to the Prophet the true guiltof Ṭuʿmah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By revealing Ṭuʿmah’s guilt, God protected the Prophet from judgment error toward both Ṭuʿmah and the innocent accused man and preserved his ʿiṣmah from sin and moral error.
rows.anchor: He protected the Prophet from committing an error in judgment with regard to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse repeats the moral reflexivity in 4:111: those seeking to mislead the Prophet mislead only themselves.
rows.anchor: This verse also indicates the same moral reflexivity suggested in v. 111, for in seeking to lead the Prophet astray, they misled only themselves.

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says Ṭuʿmah’s advocates knew their solicitation would lead the Prophet astray: revelation in 4:105 had already warned against defending betrayers, making defense of Ṭuʿmah unacceptable to God.
rows.anchor: According to al-Ṭabarī, Ṭuʿmah’s would-be advocates knew that their attempt to solicit the Prophet’s defense of Ṭuʿmah was effectively an attempt to lead the Prophet astray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other Quran passages similarly say that those seeking to lead others astray mislead themselves and that a soul’s going astray harms none but itself.
rows.anchor: See also 3:69, where, in seeking to lead others astray, the disbelievers mislead only themselves; and 39:41, where the soul’s going astray is said to harm none but itself.

rows.speaker: R, Ṭs, Z
rows.claim: Some interpret God’s bounty as the Prophet’s prophethood and His mercy as special aid or, more specifically, the Prophet’s ʿiṣmah, which mainstream doctrine attributes to all prophets.
rows.anchor: some understand God’s Bounty toward the Prophet in this verse to be a reference to his prophethood; they consider His Mercy to be a reference either to the special aid He rendered to the Prophet or more specifically to the Prophet’s ʿiṣmah, or moral inerrancy (R, Ṭs, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere bounty and mercy refer to revealed guidance for believers generally, which prevents serious errors of judgment; this suggests the terms here need not refer only to prophetic qualities.
rows.anchor: God’s Bounty and Mercy are used in reference to God’s revelation of a particular guidance to the believers as a whole—a guidance that similarly prevents them from making serious errors of judgment—and so does not seem to relate only to the specific qualities given to the prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God protects the Prophet from being misled by teaching him hidden realities and people’s inner intentions, or by instructing him in religious law.
rows.anchor: In the present verse, God protects the Prophet from being led astray by teaching him what he did not know, either in the sense of revealing to him the hidden nature of affairs and the inner intentions of people or simply in the sense of instructing him in religious Law (Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The Book refers to scripture itself, while Wisdom means religious knowledge and understanding more generally.
rows.anchor: the Book refers to the scripture itself, and Wisdom to religious knowledge and understanding more generally.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also says that God granted various prophets both the Book and Wisdom.
rows.anchor: The Quran elsewhere speaks of God granting various prophets both the Book and Wisdom

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī takes the repeated declaration of God’s great bounty after the mention of revelation and teaching as evidence that knowledge is God’s noblest gift and virtue.
rows.anchor: For al-Rāzī, the reiteration of the greatness of God’s Bounty, after describing His Revelation of the Book and Wisdom and His teaching the Prophet what he did not know, is a clear indication that knowledge is the “noblest of the bounties and virtues”
